newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh on "war footing" as cyclone approaches.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh on "war footing" as cyclone approaches.

text.p: Bangladesh rushed on Sunday to move millions of people from the path of a cyclone and the prime minister cancelled a trip abroad as the country went on to what one official called a "war footing".

More than 33,000 government and Red Crescent volunteers began evacuating millions from the cyclone's path after weather officials said it might hit the flat coastline by early on Monday, bringing winds up to 200 kph (120 mph).
"Preparations are continuing on a war footing to face the cyclone and its likely impacts," said an official in the relief ministry.
A cyclone in 1991 that proved to be the worst in Bangladesh's history killed 138,000 people on the coast and offshore islands and left millions homeless.
The air force, recalling that dozens of aircraft were destroyed at their Chittagong base in 1991, has flown all its planes based in Chittagong to the capital Dhaka.
The Navy is moving vessels to safety, officials said.
Bangladesh airline Biman has suspended all flights to and from Chittagong indefinitely, civil aviation officials said.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina cancelled a planned visit to Spain on Sunday.

Officials said she had decided "not to take her flight to Madrid on Sunday night" so that she could personally supervise evacuation and relief operations if the cyclone did strike the densely populated coastline.
The army, navy and other security forces have been asked to be ready to provide emergency assistance if the cyclone stays on course.
"Around 15 million people live on the coast and nearby islands, and it's a difficult task to get them away from the feared cyclone," one official said.
"We have already started the process because the cyclone now looks definitely heading towards our coast," he told Reuters.
Witnesses said thousands of people were taken to cyclone shelters by trucks and other vehicles as strong winds and rain started buffeting the coast.
"This operation may be hampered when the storm gains strength during the night," said police Inspector Abu Yusuf, supervising the evacuation.

Weather experts said the entire coast was likely to be swept by rainstorms before the cyclone made its landfall. It could whip up the sea into four-metre (12 ft) waves that could swamp widespread coastal areas and offshore islands.

Home (interior) Minister Rafiqul Islam and Relief Minister Talukder Abdul Khaleq held a meeting with senior officials of all ministries on Sunday to review cyclone preparedness, the state-run Bangladesh Television said.
"Every attempt is being made to avoid or at least minimise loss of lives and property in the event of a disastrous storm," one official said.
Fishermen have been warned not to leave port and coastal officials have been told to hoist "great danger" signals.
The latest bulletin from the Storm Warning Centre said the cyclone was located 470 km (292 miles) south-southwest of Chittagong port at 6 p.m. (1200 GMT) on Sunday.

"The storm is advancing at a speed of 25 kph (16 mph). It may gather momentum and in that case the storm is expected to hit the coast after midnight," Amirul Hussain, regional director of the Meteorological Department, told Reuters.
"The volunteers have been asked to closely monitor the situation and stand by for large-scale evacuation," said Abdul Wahab, a Bangladesh Red Crescent field official.
"Sitting on the cyclone's path are the ports of Chittagong and Mongla and the Cox's Bazar resort," he said.

"A deadly calm has already set in Cox's Bazar with people keeping in their homes and praying to Allah. It's already raining with a fairly strong wind blowing," said Cox's Bazar journalist Nurul Islam.
He said some 300,000 people lived in four islands near Cox's Bazar which had been virtually washed clean during the 1991 cyclone.
Many of the area's 14,000 fishermen could still be at sea, he said after talking to fishing community leaders.
Officials at Chittagong port said 24 ships now berthed at jetties would be moved to outer anchorages.
"We are taking this precaution so the ships do not collide during the storm and jam the channel by sinking," said Chittagong Port Harbourmaster Quamrul Islam.
Officials at Mongla port, where 11 ships were berthed, said they were taking similar action.
State-run radio and television broadcast frequent storm warnings.
People fleeing their homes or being moved to cyclone shelters have been asked to keep drinking water, food and other essentials underground to help them after the cyclone.
